new.n: Indian Lake: the dry old river valley south of Mankato
new.y: Before settlement (the lake still there in 1874)
new.pl: Indian Lake Rd / Hwy 66 valley, secs. 25-26 T108N R27W, between the Le Sueur valley and Mankato's east side
new.v: Whatever the Dakota gold story is about; otherwise Dakota and settler-era losses on the old valley rims
new.st: A whole abandoned river valley: the Le Sueur (or the Blue Earth) once ran north through here straight to the Minnesota at Mankato, before it was captured into today's channel (MSU 2006 "Le Sueur River Capture" study). The 1874 Andreas map still draws a crescent "Indian Lake" in it; USGS LiDAR shows a flat-floored valley about 15 m above today's river, and the 1974 topo marks gravel pits. An oral story says the Dakota hid a great amount of gold in the hills south of Mankato along the Blue Earth "before the river changed course" (one forum source). The old-channel test found the Blue Earth itself runs within about 100 m of its 1874 course from the Le Sueur confluence to the mouth, so the only real moved river here is this valley, abandoned long before settlement. If the story is true, this is where to look.
new.t: The lake bed has been dug out for county road gravel. The untouched ground is the old valley rims and terrace edges on both sides, mainly the west rim above Indian Lake Rd. Hunt in spring before the grass comes up. The pit and road land is Blue Earth County's: get written permission; the rims are private, so ask the owners.
src: Illustrated historical atlas of the State of Minnesota (Andreas 1874), Blue Earth County map (David Rumsey Map Collection)

acc: County gravel-pit and road land: written county permission first; rims are private

new.n: Jones' Ford, probable site, Blue Earth River
new.pl: Blue Earth River beside the J. D. Jones farm, sec. 27 T108N R27W
new.v: Coins, harness and wagon iron along both approaches
new.st: A wagon crossing on the Blue Earth for traffic heading south and west from Mankato, remembered as Jones' Ford (a Blue Earth County Historical Society article mentions a proposed bridge "at Jones' Ford"). The 1874 Andreas map shows J. D. Jones with 204 acres in sec. 27, with the road crossing the river beside his land, and the 1951 and 1974 USGS topos keep a road bridge at the same spot. Matching the name to this crossing is an inference.
new.t: Old fords spread coins, harness and wagon iron along both approaches. Work the low bank terraces up and downstream of the crossing, not the road fill. Both banks are private: ask first.

new.n: Cut-off bends inside the lower Le Sueur loop
new.pl: Inside the last Le Sueur River loop above the Blue Earth confluence
new.v: Anything the river carried: coins, relics and lost tools on old sand and gravel bars
new.st: USGS LiDAR shows 3 or 4 abandoned channel scars inside the last Le Sueur loop above the Blue Earth confluence, old bends left dry as the river shifted. Their dates are not known; a Mankato Free Press column (from the 1914 county atlas) mentions a 1908 cutoff, not yet placed.
new.t: Sand and gravel bars in old bends hold anything the river carried; check after high water. This is Blue Earth County land: written county permission first.

ab-camp-lincoln-mankato-1862.st: The 1874 Mankato city map draws Sibley Mound with the Blue Earth running right along its west side, just as today (LiDAR puts the mound at 44.1622, -94.0333), so the river mouth has not moved since 1874. The Land of Memories ground across the river is City of Mankato park land.
src: Andreas 1874, Mankato city map (David Rumsey Map Collection)

sf-chippewa-falls-gas-works.st: An early-1900s winter view from the bluff above ("East Hill in the early 1900s") shows the works: the round gas holder, the brick and stone purifier and plant buildings, slab and log piles from the Chippewa Lumber & Boom yard, and the Omaha Road track curving along the hill behind. By 1903 it was the Chippewa Water, Light & Power Co. electric light plant and gas works on the Duncan Creek tail race (Sanborn 1903 sheet 22).
sf-chippewa-falls-gas-works.t: The slab-piling grounds around the works were open working ground for decades; the edges by the old tail race and along the rail grade are the places to look, with permission.
